assessment: Preassembly plausibly provides an opportunity to detect incomplete kits and difficult fits, but its benefit is unmeasured. Current evidence does not establish the success targets: median time is 11 minutes, five customers reported component problems, and seven of ten unpackers succeeded unaided. Repeated three-compartment orders taking seven to nine minutes limit any account that assembly is uniformly too slow; mixed batches contain the long tail, but layout complexity and switching are confounded. Overlapping widths also limit a simple width-only explanation of insertion retries. No damage claims do not establish that preassembly prevented damage.

openings.claim: Some mixed-batch delay may arise from repeatedly identifying the required parts and checking different layouts; grouping equivalent orders could reduce this delay while retaining preassembly.
openings.delta: Distinguishes switching overhead from inherent layout complexity before changing the supplied product or shifting assembly to customers.
openings.prediction: For matched layouts and colors, grouped runs reduce selection/checking time relative to interleaved runs, with little change in insertion time or component accuracy.
openings.probe: Use reusable samples within the 15-sample allowance. Have both workers perform matched grouped and interleaved sequences, counterbalancing sequence order. Record selection, insertion, checking and packing separately; independently reconcile components to each order slip. Keep accepted-order production on schedule.
assumptions: A short bench trial fits available working time.
Grouping retains each accepted order identity, compartment count and color.
Sample reuse does not create unequal wear between conditions.

openings.claim: When the short partition is independently verified as correct, does an order-specific placement diagram improve unaided arrangement compared with the current three-layout diagram?
openings.delta: Separates placement ambiguity from missing or incorrect components instead of treating every customer difficulty as a packing error.
openings.prediction: If diagram ambiguity contributes, verified kits with an order-specific diagram produce fewer short-partition placement errors and requests for help.
openings.probe: Assign the ten participants to two comparable five-person groups using verified kits and the two diagram variants. Record correct unaided arrangement within ten minutes and short-partition errors. Treat results as exploratory. Before adoption, check replacement-diagram cost against both spending caps.
assumptions: Diagram production fits the fixed delivery date and cost limits.
Original parts, assortment capacity, footprint, exterior color and removable partitions are retained.
Prior familiarity is balanced; this small trial cannot establish the 90% population target.
